title: Ghana to Seek BRICS Membership, Asks India's Backing During Jaishankar Visit
excerpt: Ghana's cabinet has decided to pursue BRICS membership and asked New Delhi to guide its bid; the two sides also signed MoUs on agriculture and science and technology during the EAM's October 6–7 visit.
body:
• Ghana's cabinet has decided to pursue BRICS membership and has asked India, as a founding member, to guide and back its application — disclosed publicly for the first time during EAM S. Jaishankar's October 6–7 visit to Accra.
  • Jaishankar urged closer India-Ghana coordination at the UN, particularly on UN Security Council reform, and praised Ghana's role in the African Union and ECOWAS.
  • The two sides signed two MoUs on agriculture and science and technology, plus pacts on farm research and training and biodiversity conservation; cooperation will expand into rail transport, medicine production, digital innovation, and security.
  • For the Indian business community in Ghana: the visit gives official backing to pharma, agriculture, and digital cooperation — sectors both governments named explicitly as priorities.

Ghana has asked India to back its bid to join BRICS, revealing during External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's visit to Accra that its cabinet has decided to pursue membership of the grouping. The announcement — made public for the first time by Ghana's Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa while hosting Jaishankar — marks the most significant diplomatic outcome of the two-day visit on October 6 and 7.

Ablakwa said Accra wants New Delhi, as a founding BRICS member, to guide and support its application. His stated rationale: widening Ghana's global alliances, opening new economic pathways, and deepening solidarity with the Global South. The disclosure came during bilateral talks between the two foreign ministers, the substantive centerpiece of a visit that also included a courtesy call on President John Dramani Mahama.

UN reform and multilateral coordination

Beyond BRICS, Jaishankar pressed for tighter India-Ghana coordination at the United Nations, particularly on reform of the UN Security Council — a long-standing Indian priority that has found a sympathetic audience in Accra. He also lauded Ghana's influential role in the African Union and the West African bloc ECOWAS, positioning the relationship as a bridge between New Delhi and multilateral African institutions.

The visit is the Ghana leg of a five-day, three-country African tour by Jaishankar from October 6 to 10, also covering Côte d'Ivoire and Ethiopia. India's foreign ministry framed the trip as a reflection of New Delhi's commitment to deepening its partnership with Africa and its solidarity with the Global South.

Deals on the table

The two sides signed two memoranda of understanding — one on agriculture and one on science and technology — along with separate pacts on farm research and training and biodiversity conservation. Both governments agreed to scale up cooperation across rail transport, medicine production, digital innovation, security, farming, and scientific research.

Jaishankar laid out India's priorities: pharmaceuticals, healthcare, mining, defence, railway infrastructure, and digital transformation. He noted that Ghana's flagship programs — the Accra Reset economic agenda, Feed Ghana, and the One Million Coders initiative — run parallel to Indian initiatives, suggesting natural points of collaboration.

The Mahama meeting

In a separate courtesy call, President Mahama declared Ghana "open for business," courting Indian investment in pharmaceutical and vaccine manufacturing under the Accra Reset program. He cited a working model already in place — the Atlantic Life Sciences–KinaPharma partnership for indigenous vaccine capacity — and pointed to hard numbers: foreign direct investment into Ghana rose to $2.6 billion in 2025 and is projected to surpass $3 billion in 2026, with inflation low and the currency stable.

"The visit of EAM is reflective of India's commitment to deepen its partnership with Africa, and will further India's solidarity with the Global South."

— Ministry of External Affairs, Government of India

Diaspora and business angle

Ghana hosts one of West Africa's most established Indian business communities, concentrated in trade, manufacturing, and pharmaceuticals — precisely the sectors both governments put on the table this week. A successful BRICS bid would give Ghana a seat at a table where India is a founding voice, potentially easing the path for Indian firms operating there. The relationship also has recent momentum at the top: Prime Minister Narendra Modi paid a state visit to Ghana in 2025, and Jaishankar met Ablakwa as recently as September 25 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

What's next

The immediate question is how India responds to the BRICS request — backing a new member is a political call that New Delhi will weigh against the grouping's expansion dynamics. On the economic track, the signed MoUs now need implementation: joint farm-research programs, science collaboration, and the pharma manufacturing push Mahama is courting. Ghana also plans to use upcoming international platforms, including the U.S.–Africa Summit, to pitch its industrial ambitions — with Indian partnership now formally part of the pitch.
